title: SGD with Momentum
raw_sub: SGD with Momentum (Building velocity to escape local minima)
definition: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Momentum accelerates optimization by accumulating an exponentially decaying moving average of past gradients (like a heavy ball rolling down a hilly landscape), smoothing oscillations across ravines and speeding progress along flat slopes.
formula_explanation: $\mathbf{v}_t$ is the velocity vector, $\beta \in [0.9, 0.99]$ is the momentum friction coefficient, and $\eta$ is the learning rate.
logic: In ravine valleys where gradients oscillate violently side-to-side, perpendicular oscillations cancel out across successive steps, while forward velocity along the canyon floor steadily compounds.
example: Training ResNet-50: SGD with momentum $\beta = 0.9$ and learning rate $0.1$ is standard, consistently achieving superior test generalization accuracy over un-regularized adaptive methods.

title: RMSprop (Root Mean Square Propagation)
raw_sub: RMSprop (Scaling steps by root mean square of gradients)
definition: RMSprop (Hinton, 2012) is an adaptive learning rate optimizer that divides parameter updates by the running square root of exponentially decaying squared gradients, dampening updates for frequent large-gradient parameters and amplifying updates for sparse gradients.
formula_explanation: $\mathbf{s}_t$ tracks the second raw moment (variance) of gradient $\mathbf{g}_t$, $\beta_2 \approx 0.99$ is the discount factor, and $\epsilon = 10^{-8}$ prevents division by zero.
logic: AdaGrad accumulated all historical squared gradients without decay, causing steps to shrink to zero prematurely. RMSprop uses an exponential window, allowing continuous adaptation during non-stationary mini-batch training.
example: Popular in training Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and deep reinforcement learning (DQN) where gradient magnitudes fluctuate unpredictably.

title: Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation)
raw_sub: Adam (Combining momentum and adaptive variance scaling)
definition: Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2014) combines the advantages of Momentum (first moment: running mean) and RMSprop (second moment: uncentered running variance), along with analytical bias-correction factors to compensate for initialization at zero.
formula_explanation: $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$, $\epsilon = 10^{-8}$. Dividing by $1 - \beta^t$ corrects the initial zero-bias of the moving averages during early optimization steps.
logic: Adam is robust to hyperparameter tuning and scales gradient steps invariant to the scale of the gradients, making it the default optimizer across computer vision, NLP, and reinforcement learning.
example: Default starting optimizer for virtually all deep learning prototypes: setting `optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)` guarantees rapid, stable convergence.

title: AdamW (Decoupled Weight Decay)
raw_sub: AdamW (Decoupling weight decay from gradient updates)
definition: AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) fixes a major flaw in how standard Adam implements L2 regularization. Instead of adding L2 gradient penalty into the adaptive gradient moments (which distorts weight decay for large gradients), AdamW decouples weight decay and subtracts it directly from weights.
formula_explanation: $\eta \cdot \lambda \boldsymbol{\theta}_t$ is the decoupled weight decay step, where $\lambda$ is the true decay coefficient, applied completely independently of the adaptive denominator $\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_t}$.
logic: In standard Adam with L2, weights with large historical gradients had their weight decay divided by a large variance estimate, weakening the regularization effect. AdamW restores true proportional weight decay across all parameters.
example: Universal standard for modern Large Language Models: GPT-3, LLaMA-3, Mistral, and BERT are all trained with `torch.optim.AdamW(lr=3e-4, weight_decay=0.1)`.

title: Learning Rate Warmup & Cosine Decay
raw_sub: Learning Rate Warmup & Cosine Decay Schedules
definition: Learning rate scheduling dynamically varies step size $\eta$ over training: Warmup linearly ramps $\eta$ from 0 to $\eta_{max}$ in early iterations to stabilize initial weights, followed by Cosine Annealing which smoothly reduces $\eta$ along a cosine curve down to a small floor.
formula_explanation: $T_{warm}$ is the warmup step budget (typically first $1\%$ to $5\%$ of training), $T_{max}$ is total training steps, and $\eta_{min} \approx 0.1 \cdot \eta_{max}$.
logic: Early randomly initialized weights produce violent, noisy gradients; low warmup learning rate prevents disruptive initial parameter updates. Later cosine decay allows weights to settle gently into deep, flat local minima without overshooting.
example: LLaMA-3 training schedule: linearly warms up from 0 to $3 \times 10^{-4}$ over the first 2,000 steps, then follows cosine decay down to $3 \times 10^{-5}$ across the remaining 15 trillion tokens.

title: Dropout Regularization
raw_sub: Dropout (Randomly dropping activations to prevent co-adaptation)
definition: Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) is an extreme ensemble regularization technique that randomly zeros out a fraction $p$ of hidden neuron activations during each forward training step, forcing the network to learn redundant, robust internal representations.
formula_explanation: Multiplying by inverted scaling factor $\frac{1}{1-p}$ during training (Inverted Dropout) keeps expected activation magnitude identical, eliminating any need to rescale weights at test inference time.
logic: When neurons cannot rely on specific neighboring neurons to always be present, they cannot form fragile co-adaptations. Training a network with dropout approximates training an ensemble of $2^N$ sub-networks sharing weights.
example: Applying `Dropout(p=0.5)` to a dense 1024-unit classifier: on each training batch, approximately 512 randomly chosen neurons are silenced. At test time, all 1024 neurons participate.

title: Batch Normalization (BatchNorm)
raw_sub: Batch Normalization (Normalizing across mini-batch samples)
definition: Batch Normalization (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015) normalizes layer inputs across all samples in the current mini-batch to zero mean and unit variance, followed by learned affine scaling $\gamma$ and shifting $\beta$.
formula_explanation: $\mu_B$ and $\sigma_B^2$ are computed across the mini-batch dimension $B$. $\gamma$ and $\beta$ are learnable parameters that allow the network to recover the original representation if optimal.
logic: BatchNorm smoothens the loss optimization landscape and reduces internal covariate shift, allowing significantly higher learning rates and acting as a mild regularizer in Convolutional Neural Networks.
example: Used extensively in CNN vision backbones (ResNet, EfficientNet). However, BatchNorm degrades if batch sizes are very small ($B < 8$) and is unsuitable for autoregressive sequence models.

title: Layer Normalization (LayerNorm)
raw_sub: Layer Normalization (Normalizing across feature dimensions per token)
definition: Layer Normalization (Ba, Kiros & Hinton, 2016) computes mean and variance statistics across all feature/channel dimensions of a single sample or token independently, making it completely independent of mini-batch size.
formula_explanation: $D$ is the embedding dimension (e.g. 4096), and $\gamma, \beta \in \mathbb{R}^D$ are learnable scale and bias vectors.
logic: Because statistics are calculated independently for each sequence token, LayerNorm functions identically during training and single-token autoregressive generation, making it the foundational norm for Transformers.
example: Every Transformer sub-block (Multi-Head Attention and MLP) wraps around LayerNorm in pre-norm configuration: $x_{out} = x + \text{SubBlock}(\text{LayerNorm}(x))$.

title: RMSNorm (Root Mean Square Normalization)
raw_sub: RMSNorm (Lightweight LayerNorm used in Llama models)
definition: RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019) simplifies LayerNorm by enforcing root mean square scaling without centering inputs to zero mean. It eliminates mean calculation and bias addition, saving 10% to 50% GPU memory overhead.
formula_explanation: No $\mu$ computation and no subtractive offset. Scaling vector $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ is the only learned parameter.
logic: Ablation studies proved that the primary regularizing benefit of LayerNorm comes from scaling invariance rather than mean-shifting. Dropping mean re-centering saves two reduction kernel passes in CUDA.
example: Adopted by modern open-source foundation models including Meta's LLaMA 1/2/3, Mistral 7B, Gemma, and DeepSeek for optimal token throughput.

title: Weight Decay in Deep Learning
raw_sub: Weight Decay (L2 penalty directly integrated into parameter updates)
definition: Weight decay is a parameter shrinkage technique that subtracts a small fixed percentage of each weight during every gradient update, preventing weights from growing excessively large and encouraging smooth decision surfaces.
formula_explanation: $\eta$ is the learning rate and $\lambda$ is the weight decay coefficient (commonly $0.01$ to $0.1$). $(1 - \eta \lambda)$ causes idle weights with zero gradients to decay exponentially toward zero.
logic: Under standard SGD, weight decay is mathematically equivalent to L2 penalty on loss $\mathcal{L} + \frac{\lambda}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2$. Under adaptive optimizers like Adam, they diverge; true weight decay must be applied directly as in AdamW.
example: Training an image vision backbone: setting `weight_decay = 1e-4` prevents convolutional filters from blowing up on rare training artifacts, improving out-of-distribution test accuracy.

title: Convolutions (Kernels, Stride & Padding)
raw_sub: Convolutions (Kernels, Filters, Stride, Padding)
definition: Convolution is a specialized linear operation where small learnable weight matrices (kernels/filters) slide across an input feature grid to compute dot products, creating spatially shift-invariant feature maps that detect local patterns regardless of position.
formula: $$S(i, j) = (I * K)(i, j) = \sum_{m} \sum_{n} I(i-m, j-n) K(m, n)$$ $$W_{out} = \left\lfloor \frac{W_{in} - K + 2P}{S} \right\rfloor + 1$$
formula_explanation: $I$ is the input image tensor, $K$ is kernel size (e.g. $3 \times 3$), $P$ is zero-padding count, and $S$ is stride step size.
logic: Convolutions enforce two critical visual inductive biases: local spatial connectivity (nearby pixels correlate strongly) and translation invariance (a cat in the corner has the same visual features as a cat in the center).
example: A $3 \times 3$ Sobel edge-detection filter sliding over a $256 \times 256$ photo highlights vertical sharp edges by taking positive weights on the right column and negative on the left.

title: Pooling & Max Pooling
raw_sub: Pooling (Max Pooling to downsample spatial dimensions)
definition: Pooling downsamples spatial dimensions (height and width) of feature tensors independently across channels, reducing computational parameters for subsequent layers and providing slight translational distortion invariance.
formula: $$y_{i, j, c} = \max_{(m, n) \in \Omega(i, j)} x_{m, n, c}$$
formula_explanation: $\Omega(i, j)$ defines the local spatial pooling window (commonly $2 \times 2$ with stride 2), which cuts spatial resolution in half while preserving the strongest activation feature in each quadrant.
logic: Max pooling extracts dominant activation presence regardless of sub-pixel positional shifts. Average pooling can also be used, particularly as Global Average Pooling (GAP) before final classification heads.
example: A $2 \times 2$ max pooling window over $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 7 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ extracts $\max(1, 7, 3, 4) = 7$.

title: ResNet Skip & Residual Connections
raw_sub: ResNet Skip / Residual Connections (F(x) + x)
definition: Residual connections (He et al., 2015) introduce identity shortcut paths that bypass one or more transformation layers, reforming the layer task to learn a residual delta function $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})$ instead of the full target function.
formula_explanation: $\mathbf{x}$ is the unperturbed input tensor, $\mathcal{F}$ is the learned residual sub-network, and $\mathbf{I}$ is the identity matrix.
logic: The additive identity term $+ \mathbf{I}$ guarantees an unimpeded gradient superhighway directly back through hundreds of layers, eradicating the vanishing gradient barrier and enabling networks with 100+ to 1,000+ layers.
example: If a layer needs to do nothing to preserve optimal features, it simply drives weights toward zero ($\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) \to 0$), trivially yielding the identity mapping $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}$.

title: Object Detection & YOLO Architecture
raw_sub: Object Detection (YOLO bounding boxes and anchors)
definition: You Only Look Once (YOLO - Redmon et al., 2016) frames object detection as a single unified regression problem directly from full image pixels to bounding box coordinates $[x, y, w, h]$ and class probabilities across a spatial grid.
formula: $$\text{IoU} = \frac{\text{Area of Overlap}}{\text{Area of Union}} = \frac{|B_{pred} \cap B_{gt}|}{|B_{pred} \cup B_{gt}|}, \quad \mathcal{L}_{box} = \text{GIoU} \text{ or } \text{CIoU}$$
formula_explanation: Intersection over Union (IoU) measures bounding box overlap accuracy. Complete IoU (CIoU) loss penalizes centroid distance and aspect ratio discrepancy simultaneously.
logic: Prior region-proposal networks (like Faster R-CNN) ran two decoupled stages (propose candidate crops, then classify). YOLO processes the entire image in a single fast forward pass, achieving real-time 60+ FPS inference.
example: Autonomous driving video: YOLO detects pedestrian at $(x=340, y=210)$ with width 40, height 120 and 0.96 confidence, simultaneously tagging 15 other vehicles in 12ms.

title: Vision Transformers (ViT)
raw_sub: Vision Transformers (ViT: Splitting images into visual token patches)
definition: Vision Transformer (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) applies standard Transformer encoders directly to computer vision by chopping a 2D image into a sequence of non-overlapping $16 \times 16$ pixel patches, linearly projecting each into a token vector, and processing them with global self-attention.
formula_explanation: $P=16$ is patch size, $N = \frac{H \cdot W}{P^2}$ is sequence length, $\mathbf{E}$ is the linear patch projection matrix, and $\mathbf{x}_{class}$ is a prepended learnable `[CLS]` token.
logic: ViT discards translation invariance and local inductive bias in favor of universal global attention. When pre-trained on massive datasets (JFT-300M, LAION), ViT significantly outperforms CNNs.
example: A $224 \times 224$ image splits into $14 \times 14 = 196$ patches of $16 \times 16 \times 3 = 768$ numbers each, which are treated exactly like a sentence of 196 words.

title: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN)
raw_sub: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN & Hidden States)
definition: Recurrent Neural Networks process sequential inputs by maintaining an internal hidden state vector $\mathbf{h}_t$ that acts as a recurrent memory buffer, updated at each time step based on current input $\mathbf{x}_t$ and previous state $\mathbf{h}_{t-1}$.
formula_explanation: $\mathbf{W}_{hh}$ is the recurrent transition weight matrix shared across all time steps, and $\mathbf{W}_{xh}$ projects the current time step's input.
logic: Parameter sharing across time allows RNNs to process arbitrary-length sequence inputs with a fixed parameter count, unlike feedforward networks.
example: Predicting the next character in a word: when processing character 'l' after seeing 'h', 'e', the hidden state holds context that 'l' should likely be followed by another 'l' (for 'hello').

title: Vanishing Gradients in BPTT
raw_sub: Vanishing Gradients across Long Time Horizons (BPTT)
definition: Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) unrolls the recurrent network across $T$ chronological steps. Because the recurrent weight matrix $\mathbf{W}_{hh}$ is repeatedly multiplied at every step, gradients vanish exponentially for dependencies longer than 10-20 steps.
formula_explanation: The product of $T-1$ matrices decays as $O(\lambda_{max}^{T-1})$, where $\lambda_{max} < 1$ causes signals from step 1 to completely vanish by step $T$.
logic: Standard RNNs cannot connect information separated by more than a few words (e.g. subject-verb agreement across long relative clauses), necessitating gated architectures like LSTM.
example: In sentence: 'The *clouds* in the dark overcast sky ... *were* pouring rain': plain RNN forgets that 'clouds' was plural by the time it reaches the verb 25 tokens later.

title: LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory)
raw_sub: LSTM (Forget, Input, and Output Gates + Cell State)
definition: LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) introduces a dedicated linear Cell State $\mathbf{c}_t$ regulated by three multiplicative gates: Forget Gate (what to discard), Input Gate (what new info to store), and Output Gate (what to expose to hidden state $\mathbf{h}_t$).
formula_explanation: $\mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1}$ is an additive linear update where gradients can flow through time with derivative 1 when forget gate $\mathbf{f}_t \approx 1$.
logic: By relying on additive updates rather than continuous matrix multiplications, LSTM creates a constant error carousel that preserves long-term temporal dependencies across hundreds of steps.
example: Sentiment analysis of movie reviews: LSTM remembers early mentions of 'disappointing acting' through hundreds of intermediate plot descriptions to correctly classify the overall review as negative.

title: GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit)
raw_sub: GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit: Reset and Update Gates)
definition: GRU (Cho et al., 2014) is a streamlined variant of LSTM that merges the cell state and hidden state into a single vector, using only two gates: a Reset Gate (how to combine new input with past memory) and an Update Gate (how much past state to retain).
formula_explanation: $\mathbf{z}_t$ acts simultaneously as forget and input gate: retaining $(1 - \mathbf{z}_t)$ of old state and $\mathbf{z}_t$ of candidate state $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t$.
logic: GRU has ~25% fewer parameters and trains faster than standard LSTM while delivering comparable performance, making it popular for mobile edge devices and lightweight time-series forecasting.
example: Stock price or weather sensor telemetry forecasting where sequence lengths are moderate and fast low-latency inference on edge microcontrollers is required.

title: Bidirectional Sequence Encoding (BiLSTM / BERT)
raw_sub: Bidirectional Sequence Encoding
definition: Bidirectional encoding processes a sequence from both directions simultaneously: a forward pass from left-to-right ($t=1 \to T$) and a backward pass from right-to-left ($t=T \to 1$), concatenating both representations at each step so each token has complete past and future context.
formula_explanation: The concatenated output $\mathbf{h}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{2d}$ fuses context from both the start and end of the document.
logic: In comprehension tasks like Named Entity Recognition or BERT question answering, knowing words that follow a token is as crucial as words preceding it.
example: Disambiguating homonyms: In 'Apple announced a new phone', seeing 'phone' later clarifies that 'Apple' is a corporation, not an edible fruit.

title: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
raw_sub: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs & Reparameterization Trick)
definition: A VAE (Kingma & Welling, 2013) is a directed probabilistic generative model that encodes input $\mathbf{x}$ into mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and variance $\log\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2$ parameters of a continuous Gaussian latent distribution, trained using the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) and Reparameterization Trick.
formula_explanation: The reparameterization trick moves the stochastic random sampling $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ outside the backpropagation graph, allowing deterministic gradients to flow back into encoder parameters $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$.
logic: The KL divergence regularizer forces the latent space to be dense, continuous, and centered at the unit Gaussian, allowing smooth interpolation between points to generate novel samples.
example: Latent face interpolation: moving smoothly along a vector between 'smiling face' and 'neutral face' in latent space generates natural gradual transitions.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
raw_sub: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs: Generator vs Discriminator)
definition: GANs (Goodfellow et al., 2014) frame generation as a two-player zero-sum minimax game between a Generator $G$ (which tries to produce realistic synthetic data from noise) and a Discriminator $D$ (which tries to distinguish real training samples from fake generated ones).
formula: $$\min_{G} \max_{D} V(D, G) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{data}}[\log D(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log(1 - D(G(\mathbf{z})))]$$
formula_explanation: $D(\mathbf{x}) \in [0, 1]$ outputs probability that $\mathbf{x}$ is real. $G(\mathbf{z})$ maps Gaussian noise $\mathbf{z}$ to realistic synthetic data.
logic: At Nash equilibrium, the generator captures the true data distribution $p_g = p_{data}$, and the discriminator is unable to tell real from synthetic data ($D(\mathbf{x}) = 0.5$).
example: StyleGAN2 generating photorealistic 1024x1024 synthetic human faces that are indistinguishable from real photographs.

title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM)
raw_sub: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM)
definition: DDPM (Sohl-Dickstein 2015, Ho et al. 2020) generates high-fidelity data through a two-phase Markov process: a Forward Process that systematically destroys an image by adding Gaussian noise over $T$ steps, and a learned Reverse Process (a U-Net) that predicts and subtracts that noise step-by-step.
formula_explanation: $\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ is the actual added Gaussian noise, and $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)$ is the U-Net's estimate of the noise present at timestep $t$.
logic: Unlike GANs which suffer from mode collapse and training instability, diffusion models have stable convex-like regression objectives and cover the full multimodal distribution.
example: Starting with pure TV static white noise $\mathbf{x}_{1000}$, running 50 reverse denoising steps with a trained U-Net reconstructs a crystal-clear photorealistic landscape image.

title: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG)
raw_sub: Classifier-Free Guidance (Balancing prompt adherence vs diversity)
definition: Classifier-Free Guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2021) controls how strictly a generative diffusion model adheres to a text prompt versus sample diversity by interpolating between conditional noise predictions and unconditional (empty prompt) noise predictions.
formula_explanation: $c$ is the text prompt conditioning embedding, $\emptyset$ is the unconditional null token, and $s \ge 1.0$ is the guidance scale hyperparameter.
logic: Setting $s = 1.0$ yields standard conditioning. Raising $s$ to $7.0$ amplifies the direction where prompt features are strongest, dramatically boosting prompt faithfulness and image sharpness at the cost of diversity.
example: In Stable Diffusion or Midjourney: CFG scale $s = 7.5$ ensures an astronaut helmet prompt strictly renders a helmet instead of blending into general space backgrounds.

title: Latent Diffusion Models (LDM / Stable Diffusion)
raw_sub: Latent Diffusion Models (Running diffusion inside compressed latent space)
definition: Latent Diffusion Models (Rombach et al., 2022) train and execute the denoising diffusion process within a low-dimensional compressed latent space $\mathbf{z} = \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})$ learned by a pre-trained VAE, rather than directly on high-dimensional raw pixel space.
formula_explanation: For a $512 \times 512 \times 3$ image (786,432 numbers), compression factor $f=8$ yields a compact latent tensor of $64 \times 64 \times 4$ (16,384 numbers), an exact $48\times$ reduction in computational complexity.
logic: High-frequency imperceptible pixel noise is abstracted away by the VAE autoencoder, allowing the diffusion U-Net to concentrate its parameter capacity solely on semantic composition and geometry.
example: Stable Diffusion v1.5, SDXL, and Flux run diffusion on latents in seconds on consumer GPUs with 8GB VRAM, whereas pixel-space diffusion (Imagen) requires server clusters.

title: Subword Tokenization (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece)
raw_sub: Tokenizers (Byte-Pair Encoding BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece)
definition: Subword tokenization breaks arbitrary text into vocabulary chunks (subwords, characters, or byte sequences) balancing vocabulary size and sequence length, completely eliminating Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) tokens by merging frequent character pairs iteratively.
formula_explanation: BPE greedily merges the most frequent byte pair in each iteration until vocabulary size reaches target $V$ (e.g. 32k to 128k tokens).
logic: Character tokenization makes sequences too long for attention; whole-word tokenization causes vocabulary explosion and fails on novel words. Subword tokenization represents common words ('learning') as single tokens and rare words ('hyperparameter') as composite subwords ('hyper', 'parameter').
example: In GPT-4 (tiktoken `cl100k_base`): 'antigravity' is tokenized into two subwords: `['anti', 'gravity']`, preserving semantic morphology.

title: Dense Vector Embeddings & Semantic Geometry
raw_sub: Dense Vector Embeddings (Semantic clustering)
definition: Dense vector embeddings map discrete tokens, sentences, or documents into continuous real-valued geometric vector spaces $\mathbb{R}^d$ where cosine similarity captures deep semantic and functional relatedness.
formula_explanation: When vectors are L2-normalized ($\|\mathbf{u}\|_2 = 1$), cosine similarity simplifies directly to the inner dot product $\mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{v}$.
logic: Embeddings solve the curse of one-hot sparsity. In embedding space, vector arithmetic exhibits semantic linearity: $\mathbf{v}_{king} - \mathbf{v}_{man} + \mathbf{v}_{woman} \approx \mathbf{v}_{queen}$.
example: Text embeddings: 'cardiac arrest' and 'heart attack' share zero overlapping words, but their OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small` vectors have cosine similarity $> 0.92$.

title: Positional Encodings & Rotary Embeddings (RoPE)
raw_sub: Positional Encodings (Sinusoidal & Rotary Position Embedding RoPE)
definition: Because self-attention is permutation-invariant (order-blind), positional encodings inject sequence order. Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE - Su et al., 2021) rotates 2D chunks of Query and Key vectors by angle $m\theta$, encoding relative token distance naturally into dot products.
formula_explanation: $m$ and $n$ are absolute token positions. The attention inner product depends strictly on relative offset $n-m$, decaying gracefully as tokens separate.
logic: Absolute sinusoidal embeddings (Vaswani 2017) degrade when extrapolating beyond training context. RoPE preserves relative distances and enables length scaling via frequency interpolation (YaRN, NTK-aware scaling).
example: Used in LLaMA-3, Mistral, and Claude: RoPE allows models trained on 8k tokens to extend gracefully to 128k+ tokens through NTK frequency scaling.

title: Collaborative Filtering via Matrix Factorization Embeddings
raw_sub: Collaborative Filtering via Matrix Factorization Embeddings
definition: Matrix factorization decomposes a sparse user-item interaction matrix $\mathbf{R}$ into dense low-rank user embedding matrix $\mathbf{U}$ and item embedding matrix $\mathbf{V}$, capturing latent preferences and attributes for personalized recommendations.
formula_explanation: $r_{ui}$ is the observed rating/click, $\mathbf{u}_u \in \mathbb{R}^k$ is user $u$'s embedding, $\mathbf{v}_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$ is item $i$'s embedding, and $\lambda$ prevents overfitting.
logic: Users with similar viewing histories end up nearby in latent space. When user $A$ likes movies $X, Y$ and user $B$ likes $X, Y, Z$, user $A$'s dot product with movie $Z$ will be high, generating the recommendation.
example: Netflix / YouTube recommender systems: factorizing hundreds of millions of user watch records into 128-dimensional embedding vectors for instantaneous candidate retrieval.

title: Context Windows & Sequence Length Extrapolation
raw_sub: Context Windows & Sequence Length Extrapolation
definition: Context window defines the maximum sequence length an LLM can consume in a single forward pass. Extrapolation techniques (ALiBi, RoPE interpolation, LongLoRA) allow models pre-trained on short sequences to process 100k to 1M+ tokens without catastrophic perplexity explosion.
formula_explanation: ALiBi (Press et al., 2021) subtracts a linear penalty proportional to token distance $|i-j|$, with head-specific constant slope $m$.
logic: Standard self-attention memory scales quadratically $O(N^2)$ with token length $N$. RingAttention and Chunked FlashAttention distribute long context across GPU clusters to make 1-million-token prompts feasible.
example: Uploading a 500-page financial PDF into Gemini 1.5 Pro (2-million token context window) and asking targeted compliance questions across historical disclosures.

title: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) Projections
raw_sub: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) Vector Projections
definition: Self-attention transforms each input token embedding $\mathbf{x}$ into three distinct functional vector roles through learned linear projection weight matrices: Query $\mathbf{Q}$ (what I am looking for), Key $\mathbf{K}$ (what I contain), and Value $\mathbf{V}$ (the actual content payload).
formula_explanation: For input sequence $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d_{model}}$, weight matrices $\mathbf{W}_Q, \mathbf{W}_K, \mathbf{W}_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{model} \times d_k}$ generate representations $\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d_k}$.
logic: Decoupling Key and Value is the core innovation: the Key is optimized for indexing and matching against Queries, while the Value stores the raw semantic information transferred upon a match.
example: In a database search analogy: a search query string is $\mathbf{Q}$, column index titles are $\mathbf{K}$, and row table contents returned are $\mathbf{V}$.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
raw_sub: Scaled Dot-Product Attention & Temperature Scaling (√d_k)
definition: Scaled Dot-Product Attention (Vaswani et al., 2017) computes token relevance weights by taking dot products between queries and keys, dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ to prevent variance explosion, applying softmax, and computing a weighted sum of values.
formula_explanation: $d_k$ is the dimensionality of query/key vectors. If components have zero mean and unit variance, the dot product $\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{k}$ has variance $d_k$; dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ restores unit variance.
logic: Without the scaling factor $\sqrt{d_k}$, large dimensions (e.g. $d_k = 128$) produce huge dot products, pushing Softmax into regions with near-zero gradients (vanishing gradient saturation).
example: With $d_k=64$, $\sqrt{d_k}=8$. If $\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{k} = 32.0$, scaling rescales it to $4.0$, keeping Softmax gradients alive and informative.
raw_subtopic: Scaled Dot-Product Attention & Temperature Scaling (√d_k)
def: Scaled Dot-Product Attention (Vaswani et al., 2017) computes token relevance weights by taking dot products between queries and keys, dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ to prevent variance explosion, applying softmax, and computing a weighted sum of values.
simple_summary: Scaled Dot-Product Attention is the engine of ChatGPT. It compares what a word is looking for (Query) with what other words offer (Key), scores how well they match, and gathers their information (Value).

numerical_example:
Suppose Key dimension d_k = 64, so √d_k = 8.
1. Raw dot product between word 'bank' and word 'river' = 32.0.

3. Softmax turns 4.0 into a high attention probability (e.g. 0.85 or 85%).
4. 85% of 'river's Value vector is blended into 'bank', clarifying that 'bank' means a riverbank, not a money vault!

title: Multi-Head Attention (MHA)
raw_sub: Multi-Head Attention (MHA for diverse linguistic perspectives)
definition: Multi-Head Attention projects Queries, Keys, and Values into $h$ separate representation subspaces in parallel, allowing the model to attend simultaneously to information from different representation positions and semantic perspectives.
formula_explanation: $h$ is number of heads (typically 32 to 128), head dimension is $d_k = \frac{d_{model}}{h}$, and $\mathbf{W}_O \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{model} \times d_{model}}$ fuses head outputs.
logic: A single attention head can only focus on one type of relationship (e.g. grammatical subject). Multiple heads allow one head to track syntax, another to resolve pronoun coreference, and another to capture semantic tone.
example: In 'The dog didn't cross the street because *it* was too tired': Head 3 links 'it' to 'dog', while Head 7 links 'cross' to 'street'.

title: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
raw_sub: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA to compress KV-cache memory)
definition: Grouped-Query Attention (Ainslie et al., 2023) interpolates between Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and Multi-Query Attention (MQA) by sharing single Key and Value heads across groups of Query heads, dramatically compressing KV-cache memory during autoregressive inference.
formula_explanation: $H_Q$ is query heads, $H_{KV}$ is key-value heads. Each group of $G$ query heads attends to the identical shared KV projection.
logic: During LLM generation, caching Keys and Values dominates GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM). GQA with $G=8$ reduces KV-cache memory bandwidth by $8\times$ with negligible quality loss.
example: LLaMA-3 70B and Mistral 7B utilize GQA with 8 KV heads: enables serving $8\times$ larger concurrent user batch sizes on a single GPU without running out of VRAM.

title: Causal Masking (Autoregressive Attention)
raw_sub: Causal Masking (Preventing future token visibility in autoregression)
definition: Causal masking enforces the arrow of time in decoder-only autoregressive LLMs by setting the upper triangular elements of the pre-softmax attention score matrix to $-\infty$, preventing token $t$ from looking ahead to tokens at $t+1, t+2, \dots$.
formula_explanation: Because $e^{-\infty} = 0$, applying Softmax assigns exactly 0% attention probability to all future token positions.
logic: Causal masking allows training on an entire prompt-and-response sequence of length $N$ in parallel during a single matrix multiplication pass, while strictly emulating step-by-step autoregressive generation.
example: When predicting word 4 in 'The cat sat on [?]', causal masking ensures the network only attends to tokens 1, 2, and 3, preventing data leakage.

title: Self-Supervised Pre-training (Causal LM)
raw_sub: Self-Supervised Pre-training (Next Token Prediction / Causal LM)
definition: Self-supervised pre-training trains a massive base neural network on trillions of tokens of raw internet text using Next-Token Prediction (Causal Language Modeling), forcing the model to absorb world knowledge, logic, and grammar without human labels.
formula_explanation: $x_t$ is the target token at position $t$ from the vocabulary, and $P_\theta$ is the predicted probability assigned to that token given preceding context.
logic: Language is a compression of human intelligence. In order to accurately predict the next word across millions of science textbooks, code repositories, and philosophical treatises, the model must build internal world simulators.

title: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT / Instruction Tuning)
raw_sub: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT on question-answer instructions)
definition: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) transforms a raw autocomplete base model into an interactive conversational assistant by training on curated high-quality pairs of user prompts (instructions) and target assistant responses.
formula_explanation: Loss is computed strictly on response tokens ($t > L_{prompt}$); prompt tokens are masked out so the model is only penalized for response quality.
logic: The 'Superficial Alignment Hypothesis' (LIMA paper): almost all knowledge is learned during pre-training; SFT merely teaches the model the formatting style and conversational tone to surface that knowledge.
example: Prompt: 'Write a Python script to scrape an RSS feed.' Target response: 'Here is how you can use feedparser...'. Loss guides weights to produce helpful assistant behavior.

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)
raw_sub: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)
definition: PEFT freezes the overwhelming majority (99%+) of pre-trained LLM weights and only trains a tiny set of auxiliary parameters (e.g. adapter layers, prompt tuning tokens, or low-rank matrices), reducing memory requirements by orders of magnitude.
formula_explanation: Gradients and optimizer states (which take $12-16$ bytes per parameter in Adam) are only stored for $\boldsymbol{\phi}$.
logic: Full fine-tuning of a 70B model requires ~1,100 GB of VRAM across multiple 80GB GPUs. PEFT allows fine-tuning that same 70B model on a single 48GB GPU by updating only 50M parameters.
example: Prefix Tuning, Adapters, and LoRA: training domain-specific adaptations for medical radiology reports without altering the base model.

title: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
raw_sub: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation with rank r decomposition)
definition: LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) freezes pre-trained weight matrix $\mathbf{W}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ and parameterizes its weight update delta $\Delta \mathbf{W}$ as the product of two low-rank matrices $\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$ and $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$, where rank $r \ll \min(d, k)$.
formula_explanation: $r$ is low rank (e.g. 8 or 16). $\mathbf{B}$ initialized to 0 ensures $\Delta \mathbf{W} = 0$ at step 0. $\alpha$ is a constant scaling hyperparameter.
logic: The intrinsic rank of weight deltas during downstream fine-tuning is extremely small. Factorizing into rank 16 matrices reduces trainable parameters by $10,000\times$. At inference, $\Delta \mathbf{W}$ can be permanently folded back into $\mathbf{W}_0$ with zero added latency.
example: Fine-tuning a $4096 \times 4096$ projection ($16.7$M parameters): rank $r=8$ decomposition requires only $(4096 \times 8) + (8 \times 4096) = 65,536$ parameters ($0.39\%$ of original).

title: QLoRA (Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation)
raw_sub: QLoRA (4-bit NormalFloat quantization + Paged Optimizers)
definition: QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) quantizes the frozen base model to 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), backpropagates gradients through the 4-bit weights into 16-bit LoRA adapters, and uses Paged Optimizers to manage memory spikes.
formula_explanation: NF4 is an information-theoretically optimal quantile quantization for normally distributed neural network weights.
logic: Base model weights are held in 4-bit memory (compressing a 65B model from 130GB down to under 35GB), and only unquantized high-precision LoRA adapters are updated.

title: Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation
raw_sub: Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation
definition: Catastrophic forgetting occurs when fine-tuning an LLM on a narrow new domain (e.g. legal text) causes it to abruptly lose pre-trained general reasoning, coding, or mathematical competencies learned during pre-training.
formula_explanation: Mitigated using Experience Replay (mixing 5-10% general pre-training data into fine-tuning) or Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) penalizing changes to critical parameters weighted by Fisher Information $F_i$.
logic: Fine-tuning updates weights along the gradient of the new task without constraint, inadvertently destroying delicate high-dimensional manifolds representing general reasoning.
example: Fine-tuning a coding model on Python: without mixing in math and conversational replay data, its ability to solve GSM8K math reasoning drops by 40%.

title: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)
raw_sub: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback via PPO)
definition: RLHF aligns language model outputs with human intent (Helpful, Honest, Harmless) by training a Reward Model $r_\psi(x, y)$ on human preference comparisons, then optimizing the LLM policy $\pi_\theta$ via Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO).
formula_explanation: $r_\psi(x, y)$ is the scalar reward score, and the KL divergence penalty $\beta D_{KL}$ prevents the model policy $\pi_\theta$ from straying too far from original base policy $\pi_{ref}$ (reward hacking).
logic: Human evaluation of quality is easy to judge comparatively ($y_1 > y_2$) but hard to write an explicit calculus loss function for. RLHF bridges human intuitive preference into gradient optimization.
example: Turning InstructGPT and ChatGPT from toxic or rambly text completers into polite, well-structured, safe conversational assistants.

title: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)
raw_sub: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization on paired responses)
definition: DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) mathematically proves that the constrained RLHF objective can be solved exactly via an implicit reward function, eliminating the need to train a separate reward model or run unstable PPO reinforcement learning loops.
formula_explanation: $y_w$ is the human-preferred 'winning' answer, $y_l$ is the 'losing' rejected answer, and $\beta$ controls KL regularization strength.
logic: DPO reduces alignment to a simple binary cross-entropy classification loss directly over pairs of responses, providing immense mathematical stability and reducing GPU compute requirements by 3-5x compared to PPO.
example: Used to align modern open models like Zephyr-7B, Starling-LM, and LLaMA-3 Instruct directly on paired preference datasets.

title: Constitutional AI & RLAIF
raw_sub: Constitutional AI & Automated Self-Correction
definition: Constitutional AI (Anthropic, Bai et al., 2022) replaces expensive human feedback with Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF), using a written set of natural-language principles ('a constitution') to have the model critique and revise its own responses.
formula: $$\text{Step 1: Critique: } c \sim \text{LLM}(x, y, \text{Principle}) \quad \to \quad \text{Step 2: Revision: } y^* \sim \text{LLM}(x, y, c)$$
formula_explanation: Principles enforce rules like 'Choose the response that is less harmful and avoids assisting dangerous activities.'
logic: Human annotators are slow, expensive, and introduce personal biases. Constitutional AI allows alignment to scale transparently, with explicit public governance rules governing behavior.
example: Powering Claude 3: constitutional principles instruct the model to politely decline producing malware while remaining maximally helpful for cybersecurity defense analysis.

title: Knowledge Distillation (Teacher-Student)
raw_sub: Knowledge Distillation (Teacher model soft labels train student)
definition: Knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) transfers the reasoning capacity of a massive teacher model (e.g. 405B) into a compact, lightweight student model (e.g. 8B) by training the student to match the teacher's softened output probability distribution.
formula_explanation: $\mathbf{z}_t$ and $\mathbf{z}_s$ are teacher and student logits, $T$ is softmax temperature smoothing probabilities, and $\alpha$ balances ground truth vs teacher alignment.
logic: The teacher's 'dark knowledge' (secondary probabilities over incorrect tokens, e.g. knowing a cat is closer to a tiger than a car) provides immensely richer learning signals than hard 0/1 labels.
example: DistilBERT (60% size of BERT, retains 97% performance) and LLaMA-3.1 8B fine-tuned using synthetic outputs generated by LLaMA-3.1 405B.

title: Model Quantization (AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF)
raw_sub: Model Quantization (FP16 -> INT8 / INT4 via AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF)
definition: Quantization compresses model parameter weights from 16-bit floating point (FP16/BF16) down to 8-bit or 4-bit integers (INT8/INT4), slashing GPU memory footprint by $4\times$ and accelerating memory-bound autoregressive decoding throughput.
formula_explanation: $S$ is the FP16 scale factor and $Z$ is zero-point integer offset. AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) protects the 1% most salient weight channels based on activation magnitudes.
logic: Autoregressive generation is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound. Fetching 4-bit weights from VRAM to compute cores takes $25\%$ of the time compared to 16-bit weights.
example: Running LLaMA-3 8B: in FP16 it requires 16GB VRAM; quantized via GGUF (Q4_K_M) it requires only 4.8GB RAM, running comfortably on a MacBook or iPhone.

title: Document Parsing & Chunking Strategies
raw_sub: Document Parsing & Chunking (Fixed-size, Recursive, Semantic)
definition: Chunking breaks large documents into optimal discrete segments for vector retrieval. Strategies include Fixed-Size Chunking (character count with overlap), Recursive Character Splitting (respecting paragraphs and code fences), and Semantic Chunking (splitting when semantic embedding similarity shifts).
formula_explanation: Sliding window overlap ensures sentences cut in half at chunk boundaries retain full semantic context in at least one chunk.
logic: If chunks are too small (e.g. 50 tokens), they lack sufficient surrounding context. If chunks are too large (e.g. 4000 tokens), specific factual details are diluted across general narrative in embedding space.
example:
In LangChain / LlamaIndex: `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200, separators=['

', '
', ' ', ''])` keeps headers and paragraphs intact.

title: Vector Databases & Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN)
raw_sub: Vector Databases (Chroma, Pinecone, Milvus, Qdrant, FAISS)
definition: Vector databases store, index, and query multi-dimensional dense embeddings at scale using Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search algorithms like HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) and Inverted File Index (IVF).
formula: $$\text{HNSW Complexity: } O(\log N) \quad \text{vs Flat Exact Search: } O(N \cdot d)$$
formula_explanation: $N$ is total vectors stored and $d$ is embedding dimension. Multi-layer proximity skip-graphs enable searching 100M vectors in under 5 milliseconds.
logic: Exact brute-force cosine distance search requires computing dot products against every document in the database, which becomes impossible at enterprise scale.
example: Using Pinecone, Qdrant, or Chroma to store 2 million enterprise HR policies and querying the top 5 most relevant snippets in 12ms.

title: Hybrid Search (Dense + Sparse BM25 Fusion)
raw_sub: Hybrid Search (Dense Vector Cosine + Sparse BM25 Keyword Search)
definition: Hybrid search combines the semantic conceptual understanding of dense vector embeddings with the exact keyword matching precision of sparse lexical search (BM25 / SPLADE), fused using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).
formula_explanation: $\text{rank}_m(d)$ is the 1-based rank position of document $d$ in system $m$, and $k$ is a smoothing constant.
logic: Dense embeddings often fail on exact alphanumeric identifiers (part numbers, serial codes, drug names 'XYZ-9021'). BM25 nails exact strings, while dense vectors nail conceptual synonyms ('head pain' $\to$ 'migraine').
example: Searching medical records for patient 'ID-99412 allergy penicillin': BM25 guarantees finding the exact ID, while dense search surfaces relevant clinical allergy documentation.

title: Cross-Encoder Re-ranking
raw_sub: Cross-Encoder Re-ranking (Rescoring candidate chunks)
definition: Re-ranking uses a two-stage retrieval pipeline: a fast bi-encoder (vector DB) retrieves top $K=50$ candidates, which are then passed through an intensive cross-encoder model (e.g. Cohere Rerank, BGE-Reranker) that performs joint full self-attention across prompt and passage pairs.
formula_explanation: Cross-encoders evaluate all pairwise token interactions between query and candidate document simultaneously, yielding dramatically higher semantic accuracy.
logic: Bi-encoders compress an entire 500-word document into a single fixed vector, inherently losing fine nuance. Cross-encoders examine every word of query against every word of chunk.
example: In an enterprise RAG pipeline: vector search fetches 40 candidates; Cross-Encoder rescores and filters down to the top 3 truly authoritative passages, boosting factual accuracy by 25%.

title: Hallucination Mitigation & Source Grounding
raw_sub: Hallucination Mitigation & Source Grounding
definition: Techniques to ensure an LLM generates answers strictly grounded in retrieved evidence rather than fabricating plausible-sounding falsehoods from parametric memory. Includes citation linking, chain-of-verification, and RAG triad evaluation (Context Relevance, Groundedness, Answer Relevance).
formula: $$\text{Faithfulness Score} = \frac{|\text{Claims in Answer supported by Context}|}{|\text{Total Claims in Answer}|} \in [0, 1]$$
formula_explanation: Using TruLens / Ragas frameworks: automated evaluator models decompose responses into atomic assertions and verify each against source snippets.
logic: LLMs are statistical sequence completion engines without inherent epistemic awareness of truth. Explicit system instructions ('If the context does not contain the answer, state that you do not know') reduce hallucinations drastically.
example: Medical RAG assistant appending footnote citations `[Source: Doc 4, p.12]` to every dosage claim, preventing lethal hallucinated drug instructions.

title: Zero-shot & Few-shot In-Context Learning
raw_sub: Zero-shot & Few-shot In-Context Learning
definition: In-Context Learning (Brown et al., 2020) allows pre-trained LLMs to execute new tasks without parameter weight updates simply by conditioning on task instructions (Zero-shot) or a few input-output demonstration pairs (Few-shot) inside the prompt.
formula_explanation: $k$ is the number of exemplars (shots). In-context attention mechanisms infer latent task functions directly on the forward pass activations.
logic: Few-shot examples steer model activations into the desired output distribution and format (e.g. valid JSON) without triggering catastrophic forgetting or fine-tuning infrastructure costs.
example: Prompting: 'Translate English to SQL. Input: show active users -> Output: SELECT * FROM users WHERE active=1; Input: count orders -> Output: [Model completes correctly]'.

title: Chain of Thought (CoT Reasoning)
raw_sub: Chain of Thought (CoT - 'Let's think step by step')
definition: Chain of Thought (Wei et al., 2022) prompts language models to decompose complex multi-step reasoning problems into intermediate natural language deduction steps before arriving at a final answer (e.g. 'Let's think step by step').
formula_explanation: Allocates intermediate test-time compute tokens, expanding the working computational budget of the transformer forward passes.
logic: Transformers perform a fixed amount of computation per output token. Asking for an instant answer forces a 1-step guess. Generating intermediate thought tokens allows the model to store partial state and work through algorithmic logic.
example: Math word problem: 'A store has 15 apples. It sells 6, buys 10, then drops 2. How many are left?' CoT writes out $15-6=9 \to 9+10=19 \to 19-2=17$, avoiding careless arithmetic errors.

title: ReAct Framework (Reasoning + Acting)
raw_sub: ReAct Framework (Reasoning + Acting in iterative loops)
definition: The ReAct framework (Yao et al., 2022) combines reasoning traces and task-specific external tool actions in an interleaved loop: Thought (verbal reason about situation) $\to$ Action (call tool) $\to$ Observation (receive tool output) $\to$ Repeat until goal is achieved.
formula_explanation: $\tau_t$ is the historical context trace, augmented with each new observation to ground subsequent reasoning steps.
logic: Pure reasoning models suffer from hallucination and lack current environment information. Pure action models lack strategic long-term planning. ReAct combines dynamic thought planning with environmental feedback.
example: Agent looking up weather: Thought: 'I need current temperature in Tokyo.' Action: `weather_api('Tokyo')`. Observation: `'22°C, Rain'`. Thought: 'Now I should advise an umbrella.' Final Response: 'It is 22°C and rainy in Tokyo, bring an umbrella!'

title: Function Calling & Tool Use
raw_sub: Function Calling & Tool Use (APIs, Code Interpreters, SQL)
definition: Function calling equips LLMs with JSON schemas defining available software tools (APIs, databases, bash shells, calculators). The model generates structured machine-readable JSON function calls instead of text, which an executor environment runs and returns results for.
formula_explanation: Fine-tuned models strictly conform to JSON Schema specifications, enabling reliable deterministic software integration.
logic: Allows models to break out of the static knowledge frozen at training time, performing real-world actions like running unit tests, sending emails, or querying live SQL databases.
example: User asks: 'Calculate $893 \times 4291$'. Instead of guessing, the LLM emits a function call `python_interpreter(expr='893 * 4291')`, receiving exact answer `3831863`.

title: High-Throughput Serving & PagedAttention (vLLM)
raw_sub: High-Throughput Serving (vLLM PagedAttention, TensorRT-LLM, ONNX)
definition: Production inference optimization technologies that maximize GPU hardware utilization. PagedAttention (vLLM - Kwon et al., 2023) manages LLM Key-Value cache memory like virtual memory pages in operating systems, eliminating internal and external fragmentation.
formula_explanation: Continuous iteration-level batching dynamically injects new requests as soon as finished requests complete, without waiting for batch completion.
logic: Standard LLM serving pre-allocates contiguous memory for maximum possible sequence lengths (e.g. 4096 tokens), leaving huge empty memory gaps. PagedAttention allocates blocks dynamically on demand.
example: vLLM serves 20-30x more tokens per second per GPU compared to standard Hugging Face Transformers, enabling economical production scale.

title: Data Drift vs Concept Drift Monitoring
raw_sub: Data Drift vs Concept Drift Monitoring (PSI, KS-Test)
definition: Data Drift refers to shifts in the input feature distribution $P(X)$ over time while relationship $P(Y|X)$ remains constant. Concept Drift occurs when the true statistical relationship between inputs and targets $P(Y|X)$ changes due to macroeconomic or real-world shifts.
formula_explanation: Population Stability Index (PSI): $\text{PSI} < 0.1$ indicates stability, $> 0.25$ indicates significant drift requiring model retraining. KS is Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
logic: Models trained on static historical data inevitably decay in accuracy as consumer habits, inflation, or seasons change. Automated drift alarms trigger automated retraining pipelines.
example: E-commerce spending during COVID-19 lockdown: purchase behavior shifted overnight. Concept drift rendered previous fraud detection models inaccurate until retrained.

title: Feature Stores & Continuous Training CI/CD
raw_sub: Feature Stores & Continuous Training CI/CD Pipelines
definition: A feature store (e.g. Feast, Hopsworks) provides a unified data platform with a dual interface: low-latency key-value storage (Redis) for real-time online inference, and distributed storage (Snowflake/BigQuery) with point-in-time time-travel joins for offline training.
formula_explanation: Strict point-in-time correctness guarantees training datasets never leak features that occurred after prediction event timestamp $t$.
logic: Training-serving skew (features computed differently in Python during training vs in C++/Java during online serving) is the #1 cause of silent production model failure.
example: Credit card fraud: real-time feature 'number of transactions in last 10 minutes' is served from Redis in 2ms during checkout and queried with exact timestamps for historical model training.

title: Fairness, Accountability & Responsible AI Auditing
raw_sub: Fairness, Accountability & Responsible AI Auditing
definition: Auditing frameworks to identify, measure, and mitigate systemic bias, demographic disparities, and privacy leakage in production AI models. Enforces criteria such as Demographic Parity, Equalized Odds, and Differential Privacy.
formula: $$\text{Demographic Parity: } P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=0) = P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=1)$$ $$\text{Equalized Odds: } P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=0, Y=y) = P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=1, Y=y)$$
formula_explanation: $A \in \{0, 1\}$ is a protected demographic attribute (gender, ethnicity, age) and $Y$ is the ground truth outcome.
logic: Models trained on historical data frequently reproduce historical socio-economic inequities. Formal auditing ensures algorithmic fairness before models are approved for lending, hiring, or healthcare.
example: Using Fairlearn or AIF360 to audit loan approval algorithms, ensuring qualified applicants receive equal acceptance rates regardless of gender.
